etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English prollen, of unknown origin.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To rove over, through, or about in a stealthy manner; especially, to search in, as for prey or booty.

quote.citation: a. 1587, Philippe Sidnei [i.e., Philip Sidney], “(please specify the folio)”, in [Fulke Greville; Matthew Gwinne; John Florio], editors, The Countesse of Pembrokes Arcadia [The New Arcadia], London:  […]  [John Windet] for William Ponsonbie, published 1590, →OCLC:
quote.text: He prowls each place, still in new colours decked.

quote.citation: 2011 January 5, Mark Ashenden, “Wolverhampton 1 - 0 Chelsea”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: While McCarthy prowled the touchline barking orders, his opposite number watched on motionless and expressionless and, with 25 minutes to go, decided to throw on Nicolas Anelka for Kalou.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To idle; to go about aimlessly.
